major-taylor.excerpt: The fastest cyclist in the world, barred from most races because he was Black, and buried in an unmarked grave.
sections: Why 'Major'

Marshall Taylor was born in Indianapolis in 1878. As a boy he performed bicycle stunts outside the Hay & Willits bike shop to draw customers, wearing a military uniform; the Indiana State Library says his father had fought for the Union. The nickname stuck: Major Taylor. In 1895, at sixteen, he won a 75-mile road race from Indianapolis to Matthews, Indiana, and that year he moved to Worcester, Massachusetts, with his manager and mentor, the former champion Louis "Birdie" Munger, hoping for fairer treatment than Indiana gave him.
In December 1896, in his first professional contest, he won a sprint at Madison Square Garden in New York, then rode a six-day race there, finishing eighth at eighteen.
Barred, boxed in, choked

Taylor was barred from most races because he was Black, and his races were marketed as white against Black. In New Albany, Indiana, white Southern riders refused to race him and threatened him until the referee called the contest off. In Louisville he was told the law barred Black riders from even practising on the track. When he did race, rivals boxed him in and fouled him. On 23 September 1897, at a county fair in Taunton, Massachusetts, in front of about 25,000 people, he finished second; the third-place rider, William Becker, choked him until he lost consciousness. Becker was fined fifty dollars. Taylor's 1897 season ended early.

Munger, according to his own later account, once tried a skin-lightening lotion on Taylor that left him badly burned. That story rests on Munger's recollection alone. Reports that spectators threw ice and nails, and that an Indianapolis track banned him after a record, come from a single source each and are not repeated here.
Montreal, 1899

In August 1899, in Montreal, Taylor won the world one-mile sprint championship. The Smithsonian and the Boston Globe call him the first African American world champion in any sport; the Black Canadian boxer George Dixon had won a world title earlier, which is why the claim is worded that way. He was American sprint champion in 1899 and again in 1900, and in 1901 was declared champion indoor rider of America at Madison Square Garden. He held the one-mile sprint record; the number of world records he set differs between sources.

He raced the champion of France in Paris, toured Europe and won most of his races, and made two trips to Australia. He married Daisy Morris in 1902. The Library of Congress says he earned thousands of dollars a season, and was the best-known Black American in the country from 1895 until he retired, in 1910, at 32.
An unmarked grave

Retirement went badly. Business ventures failed, and the Depression took what was left. In 1928 he published his autobiography, The Fastest Bicycle Rider in the World, at his own expense, and sold it door to door. He died in 1932 in the charity ward of Cook County Hospital in Chicago and was buried in an unmarked grave.

In 1948 a group of former cyclists, with money from the bicycle maker Frank Schwinn, moved him to a proper grave with a marker. Taylor himself had put it simply, the Globe records: "My color is my fortune."

mansa-musa.excerpt: In 1324, the king of Mali passed through Cairo on his way to Mecca and gave away so much gold that its price fell for a decade.
sections: The Empire of Mali

Mansa Musa, also called Musa I, became ruler of Mali in 1312, after his predecessor Abu Bakr II sailed into the Atlantic on an expedition and never returned. He inherited a rich kingdom and made it richer. At its height Mali reached across West Africa, over parts of today's Mali, Senegal, the Gambia, Guinea, Mauritania, Niger and beyond; its wealth came from gold and salt, with ivory a further source. National Geographic gives his reign as 1312 to 1337; other sources give slightly different dates.
The pilgrimage of 1324

In 1324 Mansa Musa set out across the Sahara on the hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca. Arab writers of the time described a caravan of tens of thousands of people; one report counted 60,000, including 12,000 enslaved attendants. The camels were said to carry 300 pounds of gold each.
Cairo

The best account of what happened in Cairo comes from al-Umari, an Arab historian from Damascus who lived in Egypt and wrote down what people there told him about a dozen years later. Musa, he says, sent loads of unworked gold to the royal treasury and left no official of the sultan's court without a gift of gold, while his people spent and exchanged gold freely in the markets. The Cairenes profited, and in doing so, al-Umari wrote, they "depressed its value in Egypt". The mithqal, a weight of gold, had never fallen below 25 dirhams; afterwards it did not exceed 22. The price had still not recovered "about twelve years" later, at the time he wrote.

Al-Umari also tells how Musa at first refused to climb to the Citadel to meet the sultan, saying he had come for the pilgrimage and nothing else, and refused to kiss the ground before him. That story comes from al-Umari alone. The twelve-year figure does too, though Britannica and National Geographic both repeat it.
Timbuktu

On his way home Musa brought architects and scholars with him, among them the poet and architect al-Sahili, and built mosques and public buildings in Gao and Timbuktu. In the 14th century Timbuktu became a major centre of Islamic learning, known for its scholars and schools. Mansa Musa died in 1337 and was succeeded by his sons; the empire later declined.
The Catalan Atlas

In 1375 the makers of the Catalan Atlas, in Majorca, drew him enthroned, crowned, holding up a nugget of gold. The drawing was made by Europeans who had never seen him; it is not a likeness, but it helped make him a symbol of wealth across Europe. His fortune cannot be measured. Seven hundred years later he is still called one of the richest people in history.
